message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This brief draws on six months of trial data from three independent sources, the operator's ticketing system, its vehicle-location data and our own traffic counters, compared against a matched pre-trial period, with the settling-in month excluded so that early disruption does not flatter or penalise the scheme. The results are consistent and strong: morning bus journeys 22% faster, punctuality up from 71% to 84%, and an 18% rise in weekday boardings that brings in roughly £302,000 a year of extra fare revenue, which the operator has committed to reinvest. Just as important for members, the counters show that general traffic was essentially unaffected, which answers the main political objection to bus lanes before it is raised. We have also dealt carefully with the traders' delivery concerns through two new loading bays. The consultation shows majority support, and the equalities case is clear given low car ownership on the corridor. I am confident this is a well-evidenced, low-cost decision that Committee can take with assurance.
</author>

<document>
Policy Brief: Making the Elm Road Bus Lane Permanent
City Transport Department, for the Transport and Environment Committee, May 2026

Recommendation
That the Committee approve a permanent traffic order for the Elm Road bus lane, replacing the experimental order that expires on 31 August 2026, and approve £85,000 for permanent signage, road markings, loading bays and an enforcement camera.

Background
Route 14 is the city's busiest bus route, linking the Northgate estates with the city centre along Elm Road. Before the trial, buses on the corridor were routinely delayed in queues on the 2.4 km section between the ring road and Market Square, and Route 14 had the worst punctuality of any route in the network.

In September 2025 the Department introduced an experimental bus lane on both the city-bound and outbound sides of that section, in force from 7 to 10 am and from 4 to 7 pm on weekdays. Outside those hours the lane is available to all traffic and for parking and loading. Data from the operator's ticketing and vehicle-location systems and from the Department's automatic traffic counters were compared for March to July 2025 and October 2025 to March 2026; September was excluded as a settling-in month.

Table 1. Route 14 and Elm Road corridor, average weekday
Measure | Before (Mar-Jul 2025) | Trial (Oct 2025-Mar 2026)
AM peak bus journey time, city-bound (min) | 24.5 | 19.0
PM peak bus journey time, outbound (min) | 26.0 | 22.5
Weekday boardings, Route 14 | 6,200 | 6,950
Buses departing on time | 71% | 84%
AM peak general traffic journey time, city-bound (min) | 18.0 | 19.5
Recorded injury collisions (per six months) | 7 | 6

Findings
Bus journey times fell substantially in both peaks. The city-bound morning journey is now 5.5 minutes quicker, a reduction of 22%, and the outbound evening journey is 3.5 minutes quicker, a reduction of 13%. Punctuality improved from 71% to 84% of departures on time, moving Route 14 from the worst-performing route in the network to above the network average of 80%.

Passengers have responded. Average weekday boardings rose by 750, an increase of 18%. Over a year of 252 weekdays this is 189,000 additional trips; at the average fare yield of £1.60 per boarding, the additional fare revenue to the operator is around £302,000 a year, which the operator has agreed to reinvest in a 10-minute evening frequency on Route 14 from January 2027.

Importantly, the scheme has achieved this without penalising other road users. General traffic journey times on the corridor were essentially unchanged over the trial, as drivers adapted their routes and timings. Recorded injury collisions fell slightly, from seven to six over equivalent six-month periods; the numbers are too small to draw firm conclusions on safety, but there is no sign of deterioration.

Consultation
A statutory consultation ran from 2 February to 16 March 2026 and received 412 responses: 241 supporting permanence (58%), 139 opposing (34%) and 32 neither (8%). Support was strongest among bus users and residents of the Northgate estates. The main concern among objectors was access for deliveries to the 23 shops on the Elm Road parade. Loading on the lane is permitted outside its operating hours of 7 to 9 am and 4 to 6 pm, and the Department has met the traders' association to agree two additional loading bays in adjacent side streets, which are included in the £85,000.

Costs and enforcement
The permanent scheme requires replacement of temporary signs and markings (£41,000), the two loading bays (£12,000) and a fixed enforcement camera (£32,000), a total of £85,000, to be met from the Local Transport Plan capital allocation. Penalty-charge income during the trial covered the cost of manual enforcement, and the camera is expected to reduce the need for officer patrols.

Equalities
Route 14 serves the two most deprived wards in the city, where 46% of households do not have access to a car. Faster and more reliable buses on this corridor therefore benefit residents who have the fewest alternatives.

Conclusion
The trial has delivered faster and more reliable buses and a substantial increase in patronage, at no measurable cost to general traffic and with majority support in consultation. Making the lane permanent is a low-cost, high-value step consistent with the Local Transport Plan's objective of growing bus use on the city's radial corridors. We recommend that the Committee approve the permanent order and the associated £85,000 capital spend.
</document>
response:
# Review: Elm Road Bus Lane Policy Brief

The case for making the lane permanent looks genuinely strong. Faster journeys, better punctuality and more passengers on the city's most deprived corridor is a good result. But the brief contains a percentage error, contradicts itself on the lane's operating hours, and makes the claim about general traffic that members are most likely to probe when its own table contradicts it. The comparison periods are also not as well matched as the author believes. All of this is fixable, and fixing it will make the brief more robust in committee.

## Major issues

### 1. Boardings rose 12%, not 18%

Table 1 shows boardings rising from 6,200 to 6,950: **750 more, which is a 12.1% increase**. The 18% in the Findings, and in the author's description, is wrong.

The revenue figure is unaffected, because it's calculated from the 750 extra boardings rather than the percentage: 750 × 252 days = 189,000 trips, and at £1.60 that's **£302,400** ✓. Only the percentage needs correcting.

### 2. General traffic got 8% slower, not "essentially unchanged"

Table 1 shows city-bound general traffic in the morning peak rising from **18.0 to 19.5 minutes**: 1.5 minutes more, or **8.3%**. The Findings describe this as "essentially unchanged," and the conclusion as "no measurable cost to general traffic." Both contradict the table.

A 1.5-minute increase may well be an acceptable trade-off, especially against 5.5 minutes saved for many more bus passengers. But this is the figure objectors and opposition members will check first. Presenting it as "no measurable cost" invites the charge that the brief is spinning. It also undermines the credibility of the bus figures.

Two further gaps:

- **The evening peak.** No general traffic figure is given for the outbound evening peak, where the lane also operates.
- **Displaced traffic.** "Drivers adapted their routes" suggests some traffic moved onto other roads, but the counters only cover Elm Road. Effects on parallel routes and side streets are unmeasured.

### 3. The operating hours are inconsistent

- **Background:** 7–10 am and 4–7 pm.
- **Consultation:** 7–9 am and 4–6 pm.

This matters directly to the traders, since it determines when loading is permitted, and the permanent traffic order must specify the hours exactly. Members approving the order need to know which version they are approving.

### 4. The comparison periods are not matched

The author describes "a matched pre-trial period," but the two periods differ:

| | Before | Trial |
|---|---|---|
| Months | March–July 2025 (5) | October 2025–March 2026 (6) |
| Season | Spring and summer, including the start of the school holidays | Autumn and winter, including the run-up to Christmas |

Bus journey times, traffic and patronage all vary by season. Autumn and winter traffic is typically heavier, which may mean the bus improvements are *understated*. But patronage also varies with school terms and weather. Without a same-season comparison, part of the change could be seasonal.

The brief also makes no comparison with other routes. If patronage rose across the network (because of fare changes or wider trends), not all of Route 14's increase can be credited to the lane. A comparison with a similar route that has no bus lane would separate the scheme's effect from the background trend.

## Moderate issues

5. **Collisions "per six months."** The before period covers five months. The brief should say whether the figure of 7 was scaled up to six months or covers a different period. The small numbers are fairly acknowledged, though.
6. **The fare revenue goes to the operator, not the Council.** The brief presents £302,000 as a benefit, but it accrues to the operator. Its value to members depends on the reinvestment commitment, which the brief says the operator "has agreed" to. Is that commitment in writing, or part of a partnership agreement? If it isn't binding, the evening-frequency improvement should be described as expected rather than secured.
7. **Ongoing costs are missing.** £85,000 covers capital only. The enforcement camera brings ongoing maintenance and penalty-processing costs, and possibly penalty income. A line on the net revenue position would complete the "low-cost" claim.
8. **The consultation supports permanence, with a caveat.** 58% support is a clear majority of *respondents* (241 + 139 + 32 = 412 ✓). Consultations are self-selected, so the result shouldn't be presented as general public opinion. The breakdown by respondent type would help members.

## Minor points

9. **These figures are correct:**
   - Bus journey times: 5.5 of 24.5 minutes is 22%, and 3.5 of 26 is 13%.
   - Punctuality rose from 71% to 84%, above the network average of 80%.
   - Costs: £41,000 + £12,000 + £32,000 = £85,000.
   - Consultation percentages: 58%, 34% and 8%.
10. **The equalities section is a real strength.** You might also mention disabled drivers and blue badge holders who rely on kerbside access during the lane's operating hours. This shows the analysis considered everyone affected, not just bus users.

## The author's description against the document

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "Matched pre-trial period" | The periods have different lengths and seasons, and no control route. |
| "22% faster" morning buses | Correct (the evening peak improved 13%). |
| "18% rise in weekday boardings" | **Incorrect.** It's 12.1%. |
| £302,000 of extra fare revenue | The arithmetic is correct, but it goes to the operator. The reinvestment's status needs confirming. |
| General traffic "essentially unaffected" | **Contradicted by the table.** Morning traffic is 8.3% slower, and the evening peak and displacement are unmeasured. |
| Traders' concerns "dealt with carefully" | The two loading bays are good, but the operating hours stated to traders conflict. |
| "Majority support" | 58% of respondents to a self-selected consultation. |
| "Low-cost decision" | Capital is £85,000, and ongoing camera costs aren't shown. |

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the boardings increase to 12%.
2. Report the 1.5-minute (8%) rise in general traffic time honestly, and set it against the bus passenger time savings. That is a more persuasive argument than claiming no effect. Add the evening-peak figure, and any data on side streets.
3. Settle the operating hours and use them consistently, including in the order text.
4. Acknowledge the seasonal mismatch. If possible, add a same-season comparison (October–March of the previous year) or a comparison with a route without a bus lane.
5. Confirm the operator's reinvestment commitment in writing, and add the ongoing enforcement costs.

The recommendation itself looks sound. With these corrections, members can approve it knowing the brief will stand up to scrutiny from objectors.
